audit: The exam analogy and existing conceptual interval discussion do not provide a shared proportional scale on which readers can compare perfect small samples with a predeclared lower-bound gate. Lesson A plots four calculated two-sided Wilson intervals and a 95 percent floor. Its counts are constructed independent binary cases, with the 72 versus 73 perfect-case boundary checked by a separate score-test quadratic calculation. Lesson B displays all four cells of the chapter's judge-calibration example as counts rather than a headline agreement figure. Readers recover both 85 percent agreement and the 30 percent false-acceptance rate among unfaithful answers, keeping denominators and consequences explicit.

lessons.title: A perfect score can still miss the evidence gate
lessons.intro: These constructed samples contain independent binary case outcomes, not repeated runs of the same prompt. A predeclared gate requires the lower end of a two-sided 95% Wilson interval to reach 95%.

data.method: Two-sided Wilson, z = 1.96; independently checked by score-test quadratic roots.

read: All four intervals use the same 0-100% probability scale.
Perfect results with 72 cases still miss the 95% lower-bound floor.
At 73 perfect cases, the lower bound just crosses that exact gate.
lessons.question: Does 190 successes in 200 cases pass merely because the point estimate is 95%?
lessons.answer: No. Its point estimate is 95%, but the Wilson lower bound is about 91.04%, below the predeclared 95% floor. Gate decisions use the specified bound, not the point estimate.
lessons.takeaway: Plan sample size for the bound your gate actually uses.
lessons.assumption: Constructed independent binary cases; nominal coverage assumes this sampling model. Repeated or related cases require appropriate clustering, not this naive calculation.

lessons.title: A judge can agree often and miss dangerous errors
lessons.intro: The chapter's constructed 100-answer calibration set contains 70 human-labeled faithful answers and 30 unfaithful answers. Every bar counts answers in one mutually exclusive human/judge outcome.

data.rule: 64 + 21 = 85 agreements; 9 of 30 unfaithful answers are falsely accepted.

read: The four bars sum to all 100 answers.
Agreement is 85%, but the false-acceptance denominator is only 30.
Nine false accepts yield a 30% error rate among unfaithful answers.
lessons.question: Would 85% agreement alone justify using this judge as a high-risk release gate?
lessons.answer: No. It conceals false acceptance of 9 of 30 unfaithful answers. Inspect those errors and critical slices against a task-specific rule. Kappa is about 0.632 for these marginals, but that summary also cannot replace consequence-based review.
lessons.takeaway: Judge agreement does not substitute for inspecting critical errors.
lessons.assumption: Constructed counts, not experimental measurements; expert labels are the reviewed reference for this example. No universal acceptance threshold is implied.
